finding.claim: The /mirror endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL. The only check is host.endswith("example.com"), which has no leading dot, so it also accepts attacker-registered domains such as evilexample.com or example.com.attacker.tld. httpx follows redirects only if configured. The default for AsyncClient is not to follow, so redirects are not the main bypass here. The check is also not a real allowlist: no scheme restriction, no port restriction, and no resolved-IP check. An attacker who controls DNS for a matching hostname, for example evilexample.com, can point it at 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 or internal services (DNS rebinding or a plain A record). The server then makes the request and the response length is returned, which gives a blind oracle.

trace.note: url: str taken from the query string, attacker-controlled
weak check host.endswith("example.com"); ALLOWED_SUFFIX = ".example.com" is defined at line 7 but never used, so the suffix has no dot boundary
c.get(url) requests the full attacker-supplied URL
the response body length is returned to the caller, which leaks information

finding.guards_checked: The hostname suffix check is bypassable via evilexample.com or any attacker-owned domain ending in example.com. There is no scheme check, no port check, no private/loopback/link-local IP block, and no DNS resolution pinning. No authentication on the endpoint. Redirects: httpx does not follow them by default, so redirects are not relied on for the bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none (only a bypassable host.endswith("example.com") check at mirror.py:13; ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused)
verdict.reason: mirror.py:11 takes `url` from the query string, mirror.py:13 only does `host.endswith("example.com")` (no dot boundary, no scheme/IP checks), and mirror.py:16 fetches the full URL and returns its length at mirror.py:17.
